title: Twelve Stones from the Jordan
summary: After the crossing, twelve men, one from each tribe, carry stones from the middle of the Jordan to the camp at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up twelve stones in the riverbed where the priests stood. When the priests carrying the ark step out onto dry land, the river returns to its flood. Joshua sets up the stones at Gilgal and explains that they will answer children's questions about how Israel crossed on dry ground, so that all peoples will know the LORD's power and Israel will fear him forever.
story: Chapter 3 narrated the crossing up to the moment all Israel had passed over. Chapter 4 finishes the scene and tells what it means. The concern now is memory. Israel has crossed into the land, and the next generation will not have seen the waters stand. God provides a way for them to remember: a pile of river stones and a story to go with it. The chapter also completes the exaltation of Joshua promised in 3:7, notes that the eastern tribes kept their promise from chapter 1, and establishes Gilgal as Israel's first base in the land. Chapter 5 will continue at Gilgal with circumcision and the Passover.
historical:
The crossing is dated precisely to the tenth day of the first month (verse 19), the month later called Nisan, in early spring. That was the day on which, according to Exodus 12:3, each household was to select the Passover lamb, and the Passover itself would follow on the fourteenth (Joshua 5:10). The date deliberately ties the entry into the land to the anniversary of the exodus from Egypt forty years earlier.

Gilgal (verse 19) lay on the eastern border of Jericho, between the Jordan and the city. Its exact location has not been identified with certainty. It became an important site for Israel: the camp during the early campaigns, a place Samuel visited on his circuit (1 Samuel 7:16), and the place where Saul was confirmed as king (1 Samuel 11:14-15). Later prophets like Hosea and Amos condemned worship at Gilgal as corrupt, which shows the site remained a sanctuary long after Joshua. The note that about 40,000 troops from the eastern tribes crossed (verse 13) is one of several large numbers in the historical books; the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan unit or military division, and some scholars read such numbers in that way, while others take them at face value.
cultural:
Standing stones and cairns were used across the ancient Near East to mark boundaries, treaties, graves, and sacred events. Jacob set up a stone at Bethel (Genesis 28:18) and a heap of stones as a witness with Laban (Genesis 31:44-48). Moses set up twelve pillars at Sinai for the twelve tribes (Exodus 24:4). Stones last, and in a culture where most people did not read, a physical marker tied to a story told by parents was a powerful form of memory.

The question-and-answer pattern (verses 6-7 and 21-22) follows Israel's way of teaching faith at home. At the Passover children were expected to ask what the ritual meant (Exodus 12:26-27), and Deuteronomy 6:20-25 gives a similar script for when a son asks about the commandments. The faith was passed on not only through formal instruction but through objects and rituals that invited questions. The ark is called here both the ark of the covenant and the ark of the Testimony (verse 16), the testimony being the tablets of the law inside it.
literary: The chapter retells the crossing in overlapping layers rather than strict chronological order, a common feature of Hebrew narrative. The instruction to take stones (verses 1-3) comes after the crossing, but verses 4-10 describe the men going back into the riverbed while the priests are still standing there. The ark is the constant: the waters are cut off before it, the priests stay with it until everything is complete, and the river returns only when the ark comes out. Two memorials are mentioned, one in the river and one at Gilgal. Two explanations for children frame the chapter (verses 6-7 and 21-24). The closing verse widens the purpose from Israel to the world: God did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know the LORD's mighty hand, and so that Israel may always fear him. The note that the stones are there to this day (verse 9) is the narrator's voice, speaking from a later time to readers who could go and look.

outline.t: The command to take twelve stones
The stones as a sign for future children
Stones carried to camp and set in the Jordan
The priests come up and the river returns
The stones at Gilgal and their meaning

doctrines.note: The memorial is designed to prompt children's questions and parents' answers. The faith is handed on in the home, through stories tied to God's acts, not left to institutions alone.
God opened the Jordan so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty (verse 24). His saving acts for Israel were meant as a witness to the nations.
God orders the whole event, from the timing of the crossing to the return of the waters, and he confirms Joshua as leader in the sight of all Israel.

words.note: Even, stone. The chapter mentions stones repeatedly. Ordinary river stones become a lasting sign because of the story attached to them. Later Scripture uses stone imagery in many ways, and Peter calls believers living stones built into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5), though that is a different image from this memorial.

Ot, sign. The stones are to be a sign among you (verse 6). In the Old Testament a sign can be a miracle, a pledge, or a marker that points to something beyond itself, like the rainbow (Genesis 9:12-13) or circumcision (Genesis 17:11). Here it is a marker that points back to God's act.

Shevet, tribe, also meaning rod or staff. The number twelve, one stone for each tribe, insists that the crossing belongs to the whole people, including the eastern tribes who would live across the river. The memorial binds the nation together.

Gadal, to make great or exalt. The promise of 3:7 is fulfilled in verse 14: on that day the LORD exalted Joshua. Israel then revered Joshua as it had revered Moses, because God had publicly shown he was with him.

christ: The twelve stones, one for each tribe, stand for the whole people of God brought through the waters into the land. The New Testament does not directly interpret this chapter, but its pattern of memorial is taken up in a different way. At the Last Supper Jesus gave his followers a meal to repeat in remembrance of him (Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24-25), a sign tied to a story that later generations would ask about and retell, as Israel did at Passover. Jesus also chose twelve apostles, a number many interpreters see as deliberately echoing the twelve tribes and signaling the renewal of God's people. And the chapter's closing purpose, that all the peoples of the earth might know the LORD, points toward the mission Jesus gives his disciples to all nations (Matthew 28:19). These are connections of theme and pattern rather than predictions.
questions: The stones were meant to prompt questions from children. What reminders of God's faithfulness do you keep, and who might ask you about them?
God wanted all peoples of the earth to know his power through what he did for Israel. How might what God has done in your life be a witness to others?
Memories fade quickly. What practices help you remember what God has done so that you continue to trust him?
